cheatSheet.oneLiner: Work–energy theorem, conservation of mechanical energy, collisions, power.
mustKnowBullets: Work W = F·s = Fs cosθ (const F).
Kinetic energy K = ½ mv²; work–energy: W_net = ΔK.
Potential energy for gravity near Earth: U = mgh; spring: U = ½ kx².
Conservative forces: W independent of path; mechanical energy conserved if only conservative forces do work.
Power P = dW/dt = F·v; average P = W/t.
Collisions: momentum conserved if no external force; elastic also conserves KE.
Coefficient of restitution e = relative speed after / before (separation/approach).
Variable force: W = ∫ F·dx (area under F–x graph).

highlights.text: Scalar W = F·s for constant force.
Work W = F·s = Fs cosθ (const F).
Kinetic energy K = ½ mv²; work–energy: W_net = ΔK.
Potential energy for gravity near Earth: U = mgh; spring: U = ½ kx².
Apply sign convention and assumptions before substituting.
Work–energy theorem, conservation of mechanical energy, collisions, power.
For a 1D elastic collision of m1 (moving at v1i) with stationary m2: v1f = [(m1−m2)/(m1+m2)]v1i and v2f = [2m1/(m1+m2)]v1i.
highlights.whyItMatters: The actual result formulas for head-on elastic collisions — the single most tested collision calculation in NEET, distinct from just stating that momentum/KE are conserved.

highlights.text: Special cases of the elastic collision result: if m1=m2, then v1f=0 and v2f=v1i (the first mass stops completely, transferring all its velocity to the second). If m2≫m1, then v1f≈−v1i and v2f≈0 (the light mass bounces back, the heavy mass is undisturbed).
highlights.whyItMatters: Both special cases are extremely frequently tested as standalone conceptual MCQs.

highlights.text: When two objects of EQUAL mass undergo a glancing (oblique) elastic collision with one initially at rest, after the collision they always move off at right angles (90°) to each other.
highlights.whyItMatters: A classic, frequently tested billiards/carrom-style result for 2D elastic collisions.

definitions.definition: Scalar W = F·s for constant force.
Energy due to motion; ½ mv².
Both momentum and kinetic energy conserved.
Momentum conserved; KE not fully conserved.
e = (speed of separation)/(speed of approach) along line of impact.
When two equal-mass objects undergo a glancing (oblique) elastic collision with one initially at rest, they always move off at exactly 90° to each other after the collision.

formulas.name: Elastic collision (1D, target initially at rest)
formulas.plain: final velocities of both masses after a head-on elastic collision, in terms of the incoming mass's initial velocity

symbols.meaning: mass and initial velocity of the incoming object

formulas.whenToUse: Any 1D (head-on) elastic collision where one object starts at rest — derived from simultaneously conserving momentum and kinetic energy.
commonMistakes: Forgetting these formulas assume m2 starts at REST — if both masses are moving, the derivation needs to be redone (or use relative-velocity method instead).
Mixing up which formula belongs to which mass — v1f can be negative (rebounds) if m2>m1.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Substitute m1=m2 directly into both formulas.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: v1f=0, v2f=v1i — the incoming mass stops dead, transferring all velocity to the target.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A moving billiard ball strikes an identical stationary ball head-on elastically. Describe the motion after collision.

questionPatterns.patternName: Neutron moderation (light nucleus slows a fast neutron)
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: A fast neutron (m1) elastically strikes a stationary light nucleus (m2); find the fractional kinetic energy lost.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Fractional KE remaining = [(m1−m2)/(m1+m2)]², so fractional KE lost = 1 − that, maximised when m1≈m2.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: A neutron collides elastically with a stationary deuterium nucleus (mass ≈2× the neutron). What fraction of the neutron's kinetic energy is transferred to the deuterium?

formulas.audioScript: These two formulas are the actual payoff of combining momentum and energy conservation for a head-on collision — memorize the equal-mass special case especially, since a moving ball hitting an identical stationary one and stopping dead is one of the most visually memorable and frequently tested results in this chapter.

stages.answer: Both momentum and kinetic energy conserved.

flashcards.audioScript: Elastic collision: Both momentum and kinetic energy conserved.

stages.question: A neutron of mass m moving at speed v collides elastically head-on with a stationary deuterium nucleus of mass 2m. Find the fraction of the neutron's kinetic energy transferred to the deuterium.
stages.interpretation: Use the elastic collision result formula for v2f, then compute the fraction of KE transferred.
solutionSteps: Fraction of KE transferred to m2 = 4m1m2/(m1+m2)² = 4×m×2m/(3m)² = 8m²/9m²
stages.answer: 8/9 ≈ 0.89, so about 89% of the neutron's kinetic energy is transferred to the deuterium — this is exactly why 'heavy water' (deuterium) is used as a neutron moderator in nuclear reactors.

flashcards.audioScript: This is the real-world payoff of the elastic collision formulas — plugging mass ratios into the energy-transfer fraction explains directly why nuclear reactors use light nuclei like deuterium or carbon as moderators instead of heavy ones like lead.
